name: Biomechanical Analysis
title: Biomechanical Analysis
answer: Biomechanical analysis in choreography and motion mapping is the study of how a body actually moves, measured rather than guessed, and then turned into data a director, animator or choreographer can work with. It covers joint angles, timing, weight shift, ground contact and the forces implied by a movement, whether the body is a dancer on stage or a performer in a motion capture volume. In this atlas it sits alongside motion mapping, where recorded movement is retargeted onto a digital figure or a stage design. The aim is not clinical diagnosis but a usable description of movement that survives the trip from studio to screen.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on capture hardware and the software that cleans it up. Optical marker systems and markerless camera setups record position over time, force plates and pressure insoles record contact, and inertial suits record orientation where cameras cannot see. That raw signal goes through processing tools that fill gaps, smooth noise and solve for a skeleton, often in packages such as Blender, MotionBuilder or Unity, with pose estimation models doing the first pass on plain video. Output is usually a skeletal animation file plus a table of measurements, and the two have to stay in step or the analysis stops matching the performance.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical job starts with a defined question, such as where a turn loses balance or how a lift loads the lower back, because the question decides the marker set and the capture rate. The performer is captured, sometimes several times, and the takes are labelled, trimmed and aligned to a common skeleton. Analysts then compute joint angles, centre of mass travel and timing curves, and compare them across takes, performers or rehearsals. The results are read back against video, since a number that cannot be seen in the footage is usually a processing artefact. Choreographers and animators use the same data to shape timing, spacing and effort in the finished work.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Movement data is personal data, and a performer's gait or posture can identify them even without a name attached, so consent, retention limits and who holds the files all matter. Studios usually agree in advance on how long captures are kept, who may reuse them and whether a body scan can be repurposed for a later production or a model training set. Rights in a recorded performance sit with the performer and their union or contract terms, separate from rights in the choreography itself, and separate again from any model trained on the motion. This site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, a reminder that reuse questions in this area are live rather than theoretical. Provenance records, meaning a clear note of what was captured, when, from whom and with what processing, are the practical defence when a clip resurfaces years later.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Markerless capture and pose estimation keep improving, which pushes the work out of the lab and into rehearsal rooms and ordinary phones. That lowers cost but raises the volume of movement data in circulation, so consent and provenance practices will have to catch up with the capture itself. Expect closer links between biomechanical measurement and generative motion models, where recorded movement becomes training material for synthetic performers. The open questions are less technical than contractual, namely who owns a motion, how a performer is credited when a model learns from them, and what counts as a copy.
